title: Space Station Silicon Valley
subtitle: DMA Design · Nintendo 64

body: Space Station Silicon Valley is DMA Design's Nintendo 64 platform adventure about Evo, a robot reduced to a crawling microchip after a crash. He must occupy the station's robotic animals to survive, solve problems and recover the parts of his body. A creature is therefore both an inhabitant and a possible tool. Its movement and attacks determine what can be done next. The playful menagerie gives the game an immediately unusual question: which of the animals already present would make this particular route possible?

Each body has different characteristics, including its ability to survive in the surrounding environment. A large animal may break an obstruction that another cannot, while a different movement allows access to a previously unreachable place. Evo has to leave one body and find another as objectives develop. The environments become collections of related possibilities rather than stages designed around a single permanent hero. Recognising the useful creature can be as important as defeating an enemy, because the next problem may depend on borrowing what that creature can do.

Dan Danger remains near the damaged spaceship, assigning objectives and commenting on Evo's progress. The animal designs and absurd situations give the station a comic character, supported by Stuart Ross's music. Released in 1998, the game later received adaptations for Game Boy Color and PlayStation, the latter titled Evo's Space Adventures. Its most distinctive quality belongs to the original relationship between the tiny robot and its borrowed bodies. Changing character becomes a practical act performed inside the world, with each new animal briefly redefining the player's capabilities.
story_headings: A small chip needs another body
The right animal changes the route
A menagerie with a peculiar sense of humour
